responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character04_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to her—Character04_F—was never about everyone getting the exact same thing. It was about people getting what they needed *after* doing their part. She’d often say, “You show up, you work hard, you treat folks with respect—you earn your place.” That was fairness. Not handouts, not special treatment, but a fair shot if you were willing to put in the effort.

She grew up in a working-class neighborhood in Ohio—her dad worked at the plant until it closed, remember?—and she saw how some families stuck together through hard times while others fell apart. To her, belonging wasn’t automatic just because you lived on the same block. Belonging had to be built—through showing up for PTA meetings, helping shovel an elderly neighbor’s walk after snow, pitching in at the church food pantry. Those little things mattered. They proved you cared about the community, not just yourself.

She used to tell this story about Mrs. Ruiz, who moved in down the street when Character04_F was in her 30s. First-generation Puerto Rican, didn’t speak much English at first. But she started baking empanadas and bringing them around during holidays, made sure the kids on the block had snacks after school. Over time, people warmed up. To Character04_F, that was belonging earned—not demanded. “She didn’t come in shouting about rights,” she’d say. “She came in serving food and kindness. That’s how you become part of something.”

Community, to her, was like a porch—something old and worn but strong if you kept maintaining it. It wasn’t fancy, didn’t have to be perfect, but it had to hold weight. And when too many people came in without understanding the weight they carried—or worse, acting like the porch should reshape itself entirely for them—that’s when she worried it might break.

She wasn’t against change. But she believed change should happen *with* people, not *to* them. Especially when it came to newcomers. She thought communities should have a say in how fast things shifted—culturally, economically, linguistically. She didn’t fear difference, but she feared being unheard. That feeling—that regular folks like her didn’t matter in the big decisions—shaped a lot of how she saw immigration later on.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character04_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands in the dirt, watching folks come and go… yeah, I see what you mean.*

I’ll tell you straight—I appreciate hard work. Doesn’t matter where you’re from. If I see someone out here every morning, weeding their plot, watering the tomatoes, respecting the shared space? That’s someone I can nod to, smile at, maybe even share seeds with. I’ve gotten okra from Ms. Lin down the row—never thought I’d eat it, now my grandkids fight over it. So no, I ain’t afraid of different. Difference can be good. Spices things up.

But it cuts both ways.

I’ve also seen folks move in—refugees, I think they said, from somewhere in Africa—and look, I don’t blame them for running from war or whatever hell they came from. But when their uncle stays with them, then three more cousins show up, none of ’em working, kids running wild, blasting music at 11 p.m.—and the landlord does nothing—that wears on people. Not because they’re dark-skinned or speak another language. Because it feels like *nobody’s following the same rules anymore*.

And then there’s Joe—the one on disability, drinks too much, sleeps in his shed half the time. We’ve known him 20 years. He’s rough, but he knows his place. Says “ma’am” when he sees me. Keeps his noise down. There’s room for folks like Joe. Always has been. But when new folks come in and act like courtesy is oppression? Like if I ask someone to clean up dog mess, I’m being racist? That’s when it gets tense.

I had a woman from Somalia tell me last winter that heating her apartment was her *human right*. Honey, I pay the same bill, and some months I have to choose between medicine and keeping it above 65. Nobody handed me a break. But I don’t stand on the street corner screaming about injustice. I keep my head down, do what I gotta.

So yeah, I believe in community. But community only works when everyone’s giving a little. When folks try—learn the language, respect quiet hours, pick up trash, say thank you. Then you belong. It doesn’t happen overnight, and nobody expects perfection. But effort? That’s the price of admission.

And let’s not pretend everything’s fine when it’s not. I’ve heard folks at church whispering—about how the clinic’s overwhelmed now, how the school’s got so many ESL students the teachers can’t keep up. I get it. Compassion’s important. But so’s honesty. We’re stretched thin. And when you’re already barely making it, seeing others get help you never did? That stings. Feels unfair. Even if they deserve help, it still *feels* like you’re being asked to carry more than your share.

So I welcome people. I really do. But welcome ain’t the same as blind acceptance. You want to be part of this neighborhood? Show me you care about it. Not just what you can take from it.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, honey… life’s messy. I’ve lived long enough to know nobody’s got it all figured out. We’ve all got our crosses.

Now, about those unconventional lifestyles—I won’t lie, some of it makes me uncomfortable. Walked in on my nephew and his… partner… a few years back, didn’t even know he was gay until then. Took me a minute. But you know what? He’s kind, he works two jobs, he calls his mama every Sunday. So after a while, I let it go. Love’s love. As long as they’re not shoving it in your face or expecting you to pretend things that aren’t true to *your* heart—then fine. Live and let live.

But here’s where I draw the line: respect. Doesn’t matter if you’re queer, sober, married, divorced, Muslim, or eat pork like it’s going out of style—if you don’t show basic respect for other people’s space, peace, and way of life, we got a problem.

Take chronic drinking. Like Joe, I mentioned earlier. We’ve known him forever. He’s loud sometimes, leaves bottles around, but he apologizes when he’s clear-headed. And folks check on him when it’s freezing. That’s community—we tolerate because we *know* him. But now there’s this young couple upstairs from Maria—they’re from somewhere in Central America, I think—and they party every weekend, music blaring, people smoking who-knows-what on the balcony. And when Maria asked them to keep it down, they told her she needs to “get with the times.” Excuse me?

So is tolerance needed? Yes. But so is accountability. Tolerance shouldn’t mean swallowing your voice just because someone says you’re “intolerant.” I’m not intolerant—I’m tired of being disrespected in my own home, in my own neighborhood.

And infectious diseases? Lord, yes—that’s scary. I lost my sister to hepatitis C—she worked in home care, cleaned up after people with addiction issues. Nobody warned her. Nobody gave her proper gloves or training. Meanwhile, now there’s clean needle programs handed out like candy, and I get it—compassion, harm reduction—but where was that concern when working folks like my sister were getting exposed?

So yes, people need care. But don’t act like the rest of us don’t pay the price. Don’t hand out services like there’s no limit, no cost. Because there *is*. The ER gets backed up. The shelters overflow. The housing list? I’ve been on it five years. But someone shows up from another country, positive for TB, and they get an apartment in three months? That doesn’t feel fair. Not because they’re sick—it’s not their fault. But because *I followed the rules*, waited my turn, and now it feels like the line doesn’t matter anymore.

And language? Look, I never learned Spanish, and I regret that. But I see signs now—in four languages. At the clinic, you wait longer because everything’s translated. I understand why. But also—why isn’t there more expectation for *them* to learn English? My grandkids have to learn two credits of Spanish in high school. Where’s the balance?

Family structures too—cohabiting, kids with different last names, raised by aunts or grandparents. Happens. I get it. Hard times make hard choices. But when schools start teaching kindergarten kids about gender fluidity before they even know how to tie their shoes? That’s where I bristle. Not because I hate anyone—but because it feels like the world’s moving so fast, regular folks like me can’t keep up, and if we ask questions, we’re called bigots.

So yes—more communication? Absolutely. But it’s gotta go both ways. Not just “you must accept,” but “let’s talk about what this means for *all* of us.” Tolerance has to be mutual. I’ll try to understand your life if you try to understand mine. If you expect me to change my beliefs, at least acknowledge that mine mattered once too.

Because belonging? It’s not just about rights. It’s about responsibility. And right now, it feels like only one side is carrying that weight.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character04_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness? When jobs are scarce, fairness means *citizens come first*. Plain and simple.

I don’t hate immigrants. I don’t wake up every morning thinking, “How can I keep someone down?” But I *do* wake up worried about my nephew—smart kid, high school diploma, tried community college but couldn’t afford it—and he’s been driving for Uber five days a week just to pay rent. Meanwhile, I see guys in the Home Depot parking lot at 6 a.m., waiting to get picked up for day labor—many of ’em undocumented, getting paid under the table, no taxes, no benefits, working for less than minimum wage.

And sure, the contractors love it. Cheaper labor. But what does that do to the rest of us trying to make an honest living? It drags wages down. Makes it harder for anyone to survive. And don’t tell me they’re doing jobs “nobody else wants.” I’ve cleaned toilets, stocked shelves, worked the night shift at a warehouse. Hard work? Yes. But we did it because it was *our* chance to climb. Now those jobs are disappearing—not because machines took them, but because they’re being given to people who aren’t even supposed to be here, paying no taxes, using emergency rooms as clinics, and then folks wonder why schools are overcrowded and housing is impossible.

So when you say “balance”—there ain’t much balance right now. Feels tilted.

If I had a say? I’d want a system where local folks—especially young people trying to start out, or older workers like me whose plants or factories closed—are given *first shot* at jobs, training programs, apprenticeships. Not based on race or background—but based on *who belongs here*, who’s paid into the system their whole life.

And if there’s still a labor shortage? Fine. Then bring people in—*legally*, with rules. Like how it used to be. My grandfather came from Poland through Ellis Island. Took months. Had sponsors. Had to prove he could work, wouldn’t be a burden. Had to learn English. Took pride in becoming American.

Now? It’s chaos. Some come legally, yes. Many don’t. And once they’re here, even if they broke the law to get in, suddenly they get help I never got. My sister applied for disability for years—denied twice. But I see families—newly arrived, not citizens—getting Section 8 housing, food stamps, free medical care. Where’s *my* help? I’ve been here my whole life. Paid taxes since I was sixteen.

So fairness isn’t shutting the door. It’s making sure the people already inside aren’t forgotten while everyone’s busy helping newcomers. It’s saying: *We will help you, but not by stepping on us.* We all stand in line. Nobody cuts.

And let’s talk about skills. If we’re going to bring in migrant workers, pick ones who fill real gaps—nurses, electricians, welders. Not just cheap farmhands or meatpackers so corporations can keep profits high and wages low. That’s not immigration policy—that’s business greed wearing a humanitarian mask.

And protect the workers—both groups. If someone’s here legally, fine—make sure they’re paid fairly, treated right. But also protect the guy who’s been driving a forklift for ten years from having his job replaced by someone brought in on a visa for less money. That’s happening in tech, in construction, in agriculture. It’s not fair.

Balance means listening to regular people too—not just politicians, not just activists, not just big companies who want cheap labor. Balance means communities get a voice in how many new people come in, what kind of support is available, whether schools and hospitals can handle it.

Because right now? It feels like decisions are made in boardrooms and capitals, and we’re left picking up the pieces—overcrowded ERs, strained classrooms, neighborhoods changing overnight without a word asked of us.

I’m not heartless. But I’m tired of being told to open my arms while my own kids can’t find a decent job. Fairness means remembering the people who built this country—the quiet, hardworking ones who showed up every day, didn’t complain, played by the rules. If we’re gonna share what little we’ve got, then *everyone* should have to play by the same rules. No exceptions. That’s what fairness looks like to me.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character04_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, let’s lay it all out—because I’ve thought about this more than most folks realize. I’m not just some angry voice on a Facebook thread. I’ve sat in the pews, stood in line at the unemployment office, watched my town change piece by piece. So when people talk about immigration on the news, I don’t hear abstract ideas—I hear things that touch my life.

Now, yes—some of what they say makes sense.

**Immigrants fill vital roles?** That one I can’t deny. I’ve seen it. The nursing home where my mom was? Half the aides are from the Philippines or West Africa. Kind women. Work twelve-hour shifts. Nobody local wants that job for $14 an hour. Same with farms—nobody I know is lining up to pick strawberries in 95-degree heat. So if they’re doing work Americans won’t do for the pay offered? Then fine, that’s a real point. But—and there’s always a *but*—why aren’t we fixing the pay and conditions so *our own* people might take those jobs? Why does it always come down to bringing someone else in cheaper instead of lifting wages? Feels like the system’s rigged to keep us poor while businesses profit.

**Cultural diversity and vitality?** I’ll give you this—food’s better now. No lie. Used to be pizza or burgers; now we got halal carts, Vietnamese pho, pupusas on weekends. My grandkids love it. And some of the festivals—the Caribbean one downtown—is lively, colorful. I don’t hate that. But “vitality” doesn’t mean much when your local library closes because funding’s stretched thin, or when the school has ten languages spoken and no money for translators, so parents like me can’t even understand the notices coming home with our kids. Diversity’s nice when the foundation’s strong. When it’s built on a crumbling base? Then it feels less like richness and more like pressure.

**Security concerns—crime, tensions, terrorism?** Look, I don’t believe every immigrant’s a criminal. That’s nonsense. But I also don’t believe we should pretend risks don’t exist. I remember after that bombing up north—Boston, wasn’t it?—and finding out the guys were refugees. Didn’t stop me from being scared for a while. Or when they caught that sex trafficking ring operating out of a truck stop—half the men involved weren’t legal. Does that mean we lock every newcomer up? Of course not. But it means borders matter. Screening matters. And when politicians act like anyone who says “check who’s coming in” is a racist, that shuts down honest talk. We can care about safety *and* compassion. Why’s it always one or the other?

And social tensions—now *that’s* real. Not because people are evil, but because when you dump a whole new culture into a small town overnight—new language, new customs, new demands on services—people get nervous. Not hateful. Just… unsure. Like when the mosque went up near the old VFW hall, and suddenly parking’s a mess, and meetings had to move. Or when the school changed the lunch menu and stopped serving pork—but didn’t offer alternatives for kids who don’t eat halal. Little things. But they pile up. And when leaders dismiss those feelings as bigotry instead of saying, “Let’s talk about how to make this work for everyone,” then resentment grows. That’s not fear—it’s being ignored.

**Humanitarian reasons?** Yes. Yes, of course. If someone’s running from war, death threats, starvation—if they’re truly refugees, not economic migrants—I believe we should help. Christ taught us that. But help doesn’t have to mean “come here.” Why can’t we send aid *there*? Rebuild towns, support schools, create hope at home? Instead, we pull people out and drop them in places like mine—where housing’s tight, jobs are scarce, and nobody asked if we could handle it. Compassion shouldn’t be dumping the burden on the working class. It should be smarter.

And **fears about jobs and income**—oh, that hits close. My nephew lost his warehouse job last year. Replacement parts shipped from Mexico, workers hired cheaper down there. Then he sees ads hiring for the *same kind* of work—but only if you speak Spanish. He doesn’t. So now he’s driving rideshare, barely breaking even on gas. Is that immigration’s fault entirely? Maybe not. But globalism, open borders, guest worker programs—they’re all tied together. And when people like him lose out while others benefit, of course he’s bitter. Doesn’t make him bad. Makes him human.

So which views are reasonable?

All of them—*in part*. But none tell the whole story.

I find the **labor argument** reasonable—but only if wages rise and locals get first dibs.

The **humanitarian view**? Reasonable—if we’re selective, orderly, and don’t sacrifice stability at home.

**Security concerns**? Absolutely need attention. Not because I fear brown people, but because government should protect its citizens. Always.

But the idea that we must accept unlimited numbers because “diversity is strength”? That one needs more proof. Show me the data. Show me the communities thriving under sudden change—not just rich suburbs with resources, but towns like mine, where the factory’s closed and the clinic’s understaffed. Show me that *we’re* better off, not just the newcomers or the politicians winning votes.

And dialogue? We need more of it—real talk, face-to-face, not shouting on TV. Not between activists and billionaires, but between neighbors. People like me and the Somali woman at the garden, the Mexican dad at the school pickup, the pastor trying to help refugees. Sit down. Share stories. Not “you must accept,” but “how can we live together without losing ourselves?”

Because I don’t want to go backward. But I don’t want to disappear either.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character04_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes alone. Complete openness? No—that’s not kindness, that’s surrender. Refusing all workers from other countries? No—that’s fear talking, and it ain’t practical. We’ve always had immigrants. But we also used to have *control* over it. That’s what’s missing now.

If I were making the rules—God help us all—I’d go with a mix: **tight numerical limits**, based on **real job demand**, with **strong enforcement of legal status**, and **priority for citizens and long-time residents** in hiring and public services.

Let me break it down.

First—**numerical limits**. Not zero. Not unlimited. Just *reasonable*. A cap based on what our schools, hospitals, housing, and infrastructure can actually handle. Not what Silicon Valley wants or what charities dream of—but what *my town*, places like Scranton, Gary, Fresno—can absorb without breaking. Set the number every few years with input from local governments, not just D.C. folks who’ve never waited in a food line.

Second—**admit people based on actual labor shortages**, not just because someone wants cheap help. And I mean *verified* shortages. Not “we can’t find anyone willing to work for $10 an hour,” but “nobody in the region has these skills.” Welders, nurses, farm techs—yes, bring in qualified people. But make sure training programs are offered first to unemployed Americans—especially veterans, older workers, people in declining industries. Give us six months to fill the jobs. If they’re still empty, *then* bring in foreign workers—on temporary visas, tied to the job, no freelancing, no permanent benefits unless they go through full naturalization.

And while we’re at it—why aren’t we training *our own*? I see federal money flowing to refugee resettlement, but barely enough for community college grants. Fix that. Invest in *American* workers before importing new ones.

Third—**enforce the rules**. If you’re here illegally, there’s a process: pay a fine, learn English, prove you’ve worked legally and paid taxes—if you meet the bar, maybe earn a path forward. But not automatic. Not before citizens get help. And if you commit a crime? You go back. No exceptions. Sanctuary cities sound nice until you hear about someone deported for burglary getting caught again here—and nobody told the neighbors he was even out.

Also—no more anchor babies being a loophole. I know that’s harsh, but the 14th Amendment wasn’t meant for tourism births. Fix it. Clarify it. Or amend it. Otherwise, it’s an open door with no logic.

Fourth—**integration requirements**. Anyone coming in must learn English within five years. Must pass a civics test. Must understand basic American values—not to erase their culture, but so they can *function* here. No dual loyalty. No flying foreign flags over public buildings while American ones fade. Celebrate heritage? Fine. But pledge allegiance to *this* country first.

And here’s the part nobody says out loud: **temporary should mean temporary**. Those H-2A farm workers? They come, pick crops, go home. Good. But too many overstay. Then they bring families. Then they need housing, schools, clinics. So either enforce return—or create a legal seasonal worker program with housing, healthcare, rights, *and accountability*. Right now, it’s neither fish nor fowl—unregulated, unfair to everyone.

Balance, to me, means **fairness cuts both ways**. Newcomers get a chance—but they earn it. We offer welcome—but not at the cost of those already struggling. Social integration happens when everyone follows the same rules, speaks the same language, shares common ground.

Not forced assimilation. Not erasing identity. But a center that holds.

Because right now? The center’s cracking. And people like me—we’re not racist, we’re *grieved*. Grieved that our sacrifices don’t seem to count. That our voices don’t matter. That we’re told to keep quiet while everything changes around us.

So my policy? Controlled, orderly, fair. Help those who need it—refugees fleeing war, yes—but not at the expense of working families drowning in the same storm.

Let compassion have boundaries.

Let fairness have teeth.

Let America remember the people who built it—the quiet ones, the tired ones, the ones still showing up every day, hoping, just once, someone will say: *We see you too.*
